claims.subject: tamil_final_vedaviyasar
claims.summary: The Alavaivādi tells Maṇimēkalai that the Vaidika tradition follows these named sages.
claims.speaker: Alavaivādi in quoted speech
claims.note: The named figures are authorities in the interlocutor’s account; this does not establish authorship or identity beyond the passage.

claims.subject: tamil_final_brugarpathi
claims.summary: The Alavaivādi names these authors while enumerating philosophical schools and modes of knowledge.
claims.speaker: Alavaivādi in quoted speech
claims.note: Hart’s passage does not map every listed author one-to-one onto each school or epistemic term. “Sivan” here is the named philosophical author in this list; it is not merged with the deity Śiva.

claims.subject: tamil_final_markalikosalar
claims.summary: The Ajivakavādi attributes the book called Markali to Markalikosalar.
claims.speaker: Ajivakavādi in quoted speech
claims.note: The book is a text node, not a person; the name is taken from Hart’s canto text, not an explanatory footnote.

claims.subject: rama
claims.summary: The lesson says that inferring Rāvaṇa’s defeat follows from the statement that Rāma won the war.
claims.speaker: Alavaivādi in quoted speech
claims.note: Passage-level evidence from Hart’s English translation; this is a textual witness, not independent historical evidence.

claims.subject: siva
claims.summary: The Shaiva interlocutor describes Śiva as creator and destroyer and the highest god.
claims.speaker: Shaivavādi in quoted speech
claims.note: The interlocutor is not individually named; no node is created for that role.

claims.subject: tamil_final_brahma
claims.summary: The Brahmavādi says that Brahma created the worlds.
claims.speaker: Brahmavādi in quoted speech
claims.note: The speaker is an unnamed role, not a named person node.

claims.subject: tamil_final_vishnu
claims.summary: The Vaishnavavādi identifies ocean-colored Vishnu, also called Nārāyaṇan, as protector of the world.
claims.speaker: Vaishnavavādi in quoted speech
claims.note: Vishnu and Nārāyaṇan are treated as one deity in this passage; the speaker is unnamed.

claims.subject: indra
claims.summary: The Nikandavādi says Indra worships the deity of his tradition.
claims.speaker: Nikandavādi in quoted speech
claims.note: The deity praised by the Nikandavādi is unnamed; no deity node is inferred from this passage.

claims.subject: tamil_final_masathuvan
claims.summary: The narrator identifies Māsāthuvān as Kovalan’s father and Maṇimēkalai’s grandfather.
claims.speaker: Narrator
claims.note: Passage-level evidence from Hart’s English translation; this is a textual witness, not independent historical evidence.

claims.subject: tamil_manimekalai_heroine
claims.summary: Maṇimēkalai recounts her life to Māsāthuvān, explicitly identified as her grandfather.
claims.speaker: Narrator
claims.note: Passage-level evidence from Hart’s English translation; this is a textual witness, not independent historical evidence.

claims.subject: tamil_final_kudakko_ceeraladan
claims.summary: Māsāthuvān recounts that he reached Vanji while Kudakko Ceeralādan was king and hosted returning Sāranar sages.
claims.speaker: Māsāthuvān in quoted speech
claims.note: The passage names the king and Māsāthuvān; the sages are plural and not individually named.

claims.subject: tamil_kovalan
claims.summary: The Sāranar sages tell Kudakko Ceeralādan that Kovalan was his ancestor and a friend of the king.
claims.speaker: Sāranar sages, reported by Māsāthuvān
claims.note: Passage-level evidence from Hart’s English translation; this is a textual witness, not independent historical evidence.

claims.subject: tamil_final_ilankilli
claims.summary: The passage calls Ilangilli the younger brother of Killi and says he built the temple in Kanchi.
claims.speaker: Narrator
claims.note: The canto names Killi but does not establish that this Killi is Nedumudikkilli or Killivalai elsewhere in the epic; kept source-local pending Tamil-language identity review.

claims.subject: tamil_final_ilankilli
claims.summary: Maṇimekalai sees the temple built by Ilangilli in Kanchi.
claims.speaker: Narrator
claims.note: Passage-level evidence from Hart’s English translation; this is a textual witness, not independent historical evidence.

claims.subject: tamil_manimekalai_heroine
claims.summary: After a guard reports her arrival, Ilangilli meets Maṇimekalai and asks about the famine.
claims.speaker: Narrator
claims.note: Passage-level evidence from Hart’s English translation; this is a textual witness, not independent historical evidence.

claims.subject: indra
claims.summary: Ilangilli recounts a goddess’s prophecy that Indra will order Varuṇa to bring rain after Maṇimekalai arrives.
claims.speaker: Ilangilli in quoted speech
claims.note: Reported prophecy; the unnamed goddess is not assigned an identity.

claims.subject: tamil_aravanar
claims.summary: Aravanar begins the story of Peelivalai and the lost child while teaching Maṇimekalai.
claims.speaker: Narrator
claims.note: The translation’s canto heading also names Killivalai/Nedungilli, but the primary verse begins with Killi; this batch does not assert that either matches the distinct Nedumudikkilli node from canto 25.

claims.subject: tamil_later_peelivalai
claims.summary: The story says Peelivalai bore a baby boy.
claims.speaker: Aravanar, narrating
claims.note: Passage-level evidence from Hart’s English translation; this is a textual witness, not independent historical evidence.

claims.subject: tamil_later_peelivalai
claims.summary: Peelivalai gives her child to a carpet merchant, identified by Tamil name Kambala Chetti in the verse.
claims.speaker: Aravanar, narrating
claims.note: Hart’s English renders the role as “carpet merchant”; the personal name Kambala Chetti is visible in the Tamil verse in this same canto. The child remains unnamed.

claims.subject: tamil_later_nedumudikkilli
claims.summary: The king searches for the lost child and forgets the Indra festival, prompting the goddess’s curse in the narrated story.
claims.speaker: Aravanar, narrating
claims.note: The canto’s English summary calls the king Nedungilli and separately labels him Killivalai; the Tamil verse uses Killi. Existing canto 25 Nedumudikkilli is not merged with this narrative king here.

claims.subject: tamil_goddess_manimekalai
claims.summary: Aravanar explains that the goddess Maṇimēkalai cursed Pukār after the Indra festival was omitted.
claims.speaker: Aravanar, narrating
claims.note: The goddess is distinct from the heroine Maṇimekalai; do not conflate the deity and person.

claims.subject: tamil_goddess_manimekalai
claims.summary: The goddess came to Mādhavi in a dream and explained the reason for the heroine’s name.
claims.speaker: Aravanar, narrating
claims.note: This is the goddess Maṇimēkalai speaking in a reported dream; it does not identify her with the heroine.

claims.subject: tamil_final_deepathilahai
claims.summary: Deepathilahai, worshipper of the Buddha Peedihai, urges the heroine’s mothers to leave Pukār because she expects its destruction.
claims.speaker: Aravanar, narrating
claims.note: The existing Deepathilahai person ID is reused; this is not a previous-birth alias.

claims.subject: tamil_final_buddha
claims.summary: Maṇimekalai takes refuge in and worships the Buddha, dharma, and sangha.
claims.speaker: Narrator
claims.note: Buddha is a person/teacher; dharma and sangha are not represented as people here.

claims.subject: tamil_aravanar
claims.summary: Aravanar expounds the Buddha’s teaching to Maṇimekalai.
claims.speaker: Narrator
claims.note: Passage-level evidence from Hart’s English translation; this is a textual witness, not independent historical evidence. Canto 30 acknowledges that she knows prior births but names no prior-birth persona here; keep existing alias nodes such as tamil_lakshmi_past separate and add no unsupported rebirth edge.

claims.subject: tamil_final_buddha
claims.summary: Aravanar describes the Buddha’s teaching and Maṇimekalai’s refuge in it.
claims.speaker: Aravanar in quoted speech
claims.note: The teaching is recounted by Aravanar; this is not a narrated direct meeting between Buddha and Maṇimekalai.
